The house resumed, from Monday, May 8, consideration in committee of Bill No. 7, to incorporate Alberta Natural Gas Company- Mr. Maybank

Mr. Dion in the chair.
On section 1-Incorporation.

Mr. Chairman, in the few minutes that I was speaking on the bill last night I had referred to the provisions of the Electricity and Fluid Exportation Act passed in 1907 and still the law governing the exportation of gas or other power from Canada. I had read the two sections directly affecting this discussion, sections 5 and 6, just before adjournment last night. I had pointed out that under those sections no person or corporation may construct any pipe line which has as its purpose the export of power, electricity or any fluid, without a licence granted by the government of Canada. It is in relation to that very clear provision of the Electricity and Fluid Exportation Act that I should like to read briefly from the statement of the Prime Minister on Friday, May 5, as reported at page 2228 of Hansard.
These are his words:
Parliament last year determined that this matter would be one to be turned over to the board of transport commissioners; and for the government to attempt to usurp the functions of the board of transport commissioners would be contempt of the will of parliament expressed in the Pipe Lines Act.
Further, on page 2229 the Prime Minister said:
By that statute parliament placed jurisdiction and responsibility for considering the whole question upon the board of transport commissioners.
[Mr. Winkler.l
I can only conclude that the Prime Minister was speaking without adequate consideration, because the words I have quoted are directly contrary to the actual situation. The bill passed last year, under which the present bills are brought before parliament to incorporate pipe line companies, did not by any stretch of the imagination place the whole jurisdiction and responsibility in the hands of the board of transport commissioners. That has been very definitely decided outside this parliament since that act was passed so hastily, with so little information and so little understanding of its effects, when it came before this house last spring. As hon. members who were present at that time will recall, and as hon. members who have been listening to this extended debate for some time, some of them very impatiently, will remember, one of the companies that received incorporation by statute was the Interprovincial Pipe Line Company. That company sought authority from the board of transport commissioners to construct a pipe line which among other things would have provided for the export of gas and oil. On September 12 of last year the board gave its judgment on that application, and I wish to read into the record the latter part of that judgment, which has a bearing on any clear understanding of what is the actual relationship of the board of transport commissioners to this whole question of final authority over the routing of the line and the export of gas and oil. The judgment states:
It will be necessary for the Interprovinclal Company to have from the governor in council a licence to construct a pipe line which will carry the oil outside Canada and (2) that it will be necessary for the Imperial Oil Company to have a licence for the export of oil.
The acting deputy minister of the Department of Trade and Commerce was represented at the hearing by the assistant deputy minister of that department, and he indicated positively to the board that the Department of Trade and Commerce favourably considered the proposed pipe line and furnished the necessary recommendations. Here are Mr. Master's words:
"Mr. Chairman, I wish to state now definitely that any application that is required for the export from the Department of Trade and Commerce will be issued by the department-any permit that is required-and that the department favours the project in accordance with the applications. I wish to make that a positive and definite statement.
The Chief Commissioner:	Have you any comments, Mr. Coyne, with respect to that assurance?

No.
The Chief Commissioner:	I suppose that covers
the licence to construct to the border, the two licences?

Yes, both."
This board therefore approves the application and a formal order to that effect (the said line to be completed on or before the 31st day of October, 1951) will issue as soon as certified copies of said licences have been filed with the board's secretary.

That judgment was perfectly clear. The board of transport commissioners have no authority to approve or otherwise where export is involved until, under section 6 of the Electricity and Fluid Exportation Act, the government has granted an appropriate licence and approved the project. With that judgment of September 12 before them the government dealt with this subject on September 13, the following day. This is a certified true copy of the minutes of that meeting of the committee of the privy council:
The committee of the privy council have had before them a report from the Minister of Trade and Commerce representing:
That under the provisions of the Electricity and Fluid Exportation Act, revised statutes of Canada, 1927, chapter 54, no person shall, without a licence, construct or place in position any line of wire or other conductor for the exportation of power, or any pipe line or other like contrivance for the exportation of fluid:
That an application has been received from Interprovincial Pipe Line Company of Edmonton, Alberta, to construct a pipe line for the export of crude oil to connect at the border of Canada and the United States of America at or near Gretna, Manitoba, with a pipe line to be constructed in the United States:
That, in the opinion of the minister, the construction of the pipe line by Interprovincial Pipe Line Company is in the national interests of Canada.
The committee, therefore, on the recommendation of the Minister of Trade and Commerce, advise that under the provisions of the Electricity and Fluid Exportation Act, a licence, in accordance with the form attached hereto, to construct a pipe line to connect at the border of Canada and the United States of America at or near Gretna, Manitoba, with a pipe line to be constructed in the United States, be granted to Interprovincial Pipe Line Company of Edmonton, Alberta, accordingly.
Having regard to the statement by the Prime Minister on Friday last that it would be contempt of the will of parliament if the government sought to exercise some control over this matter, let me read the licence that was issued by the deputy minister of trade and commerce in accordance with that decision:
Pursuant to order in council-of the-day of-
I am simply placing the form on record. -Interprovincial Pipe Line Company, carrying on business in the city of Edmonton in the province of Alberta, is hereby licensed to construct a pipe line for the exportation of crude oil, the said line to connect at the boundary of Canada and the United States of America at or near Gretna, Manitoba, with a pipe line to be constructed in the United States-
These are the words I wish to emphasize. -as shown on a plan filed with the Department of Trade and Commerce on September 10, 1949. This licence covers the construction of one pipe line with an inside diameter of pipes of approximately 177/u inches . . .
Then it goes on with various details as to the type of pipe line, the location, and
Alberta Natural Gas Company as to this line being carried through Saskatchewan and Manitoba to Superior, Wisconsin. The point I should like to make, and that I should like to impress upon the members of this house, is that before the board of transport commissioners was in a position to consider the exercise of its authority the government had before it a plan showing where the line was to go, and it was the government that approved the actual route and location of the pipe line. They issued that certificate and recommendation upon which the board of transport commissioners acted. For that reason, it is quite clear from the record of the proceedings in the case of the Interprovincial Pipe Line Company, which obtained its authority under the very act to which the Prime Minister was referring, that it is the executive of this parliament which has the real authority to say where a pipe line will go, and under what terms it will be constructed, where any question of export arises.
It was only after these steps had been taken that the board of transport commissioners finally acted on this matter. It was on Thursday, September 15, 1949, that they issued the following order. I shall quote the body of that order dated September 15, 1949, and I do so because this completes the actual transaction which gave the Interprovincial Pipe Line Company the authority to proceed.
Upon hearing the application at the sittings of the board held in Ottawa, September 8 and 12, 1949, in the presence of counsel and representatives for the applicant, the province of Alberta, the Department of Trade and Commerce, the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, the city of Port Arthur and the board of trade of Fort William, . . .
It is ordered that leave be, and it is hereby, granted to the Interprovincial Pipe Line Company to construct a pipe line for the transportation of oil from a point in the vicinity of the city of Regina, in the province of Saskatchewan, to a point in the vicinity of the village of Gretna, in the province of Manitoba; the said pipe line to be constructed and completed on or before October 31, 1951.
That order was signed by Mr. Archibald, chief commissioner of the Board of Transport Commissioners for Canada.
In the event that -there be any suggestion that this procedure related only to the Interprovincial Pipe Line Company, I would point out that exactly the same procedure was followed when the Westcoast Transmission Company Limited made application to the board of transport commissioners. On September 21 the board announced that it could not deal with the application on the ground that permission to export would be required from the federal authorities if the pipe line were to be built, in view of the fact that export was an incident of the running of this pipe line. Therefore we have this as an established

Alberta Natural Gas Company practice. We know that these applicants in each case contemplate the export of gas or oil, or both, no matter what arrangement may be made for the construction of a pipe line within Canada and the use of that gas and oil, or both, in Canada. That leaves in the hands of the government the ultimate responsibility for the actual decision, although in the sequence of time the last order which is made is the order made by the board of transport commissioners. But as has been decided in the case of the Interprovincial Pipe Line, which did ultimately receive authority to construct its pipe line, and as in the case of the Westcoast Transmission, which did not receive authority, the board of transport commissioners made it clear beyond any shadow of a doubt that the government must exercise its judgment under section 6 of the Electricity and Fluid Exportation Act.
In view of the repeated suggestions which have been made, first of all by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) and other ministers when this bill was in second reading, that we should just let it go through second reading and trust to the committee, which denied the full information when it did get there, and now that it has passed there the Prime Minister tells us we should let it go to the board of transport commissioners because they are the ones who can deal with it, it is interesting to go back to see how different an opinion was held on earlier occasions by another prime minister of this government. This subject of the effect of the Electricity and Fluid Exportation Act was under consideration in this house on March 10, 1938. At that time the then prime minister of Canada had introduced a bill, which was Bill No. 21 of that session, and which was approved by the House of Commons on March 25, 1938. That bill was passed for the purpose of bringing the control of export in detail before the parliament of Canada. Actually, that bill did not come into effect. It did not pass the Senate. I might explain that it was not one of those rare occasions when the Senate has exercised authority of this kind, but the bill did not proceed because of a letter received from Mr. Cordell Hull, then secretary of state for the United States. This letter informed the government of Canada that, with circumstances as they were at that particular time, it was not the intention of the government of the United States to press for the export of power to that country. There were reasons which were obvious in relation to the date of the bill itself why both countries needed all the available electric power they had.
It is interesting to read the views expressed by the prime minister of those days, whose

opinions have been acclaimed on many occasions by those who are now so openly making this, in effect, a government bill. Mr. King is reported at page 1196 of the Hansard of that session to have read into the record a quotation from the Ottawa Citizen; and the Ottawa Citizen of May 5, 1925, to which he referred had this heading which is very significant in the light of the discussion that has taken place here. This was the heading: "Places Interest of Canada First on Power Issue". Then the Citizen of May 5, 1925, quoted by Mr. King in 1938, had this to say: Premier King Says This Chief Consideration in Reaching Decision on Export Question.
Deputation Urges Carillon Scheme.
Prime Minister Says It's National Problem.
Cabinet to Discuss It.
That the future of Canada would be the first consideration in the question of permitting the export of electrical energy to United States was stated by the Prime Minister yesterday afternoon in replying to a large and representative delegation from the the municipalities bordering on the Ottawa river. The delegates came to urge the administration to grant permission to export power fVom the proposed development at Carillon . . .
The Prime Minister replied that the problem which the government had to consider was not local to the Ottawa valley, but had its national, international, and interprovincial viewpoints. The government had only one desire, namely, to further the public interest. When private interest could be helped without injuring the public interest, it was desirable to help it also.
The main question for the government was to decide for the public interest, and in the export of power it was necessary to see that the future of the country was not prejudiced in any way.
It surely is significant and interesting, Mr. Speaker, that the prime minister who preceded the present Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) expressed an opinion which was condensed into these words: "Places interest of Canada first on power issue". That is exactly the view that has been stressed in the discussion that has taken place here since these bills originally came before the house. From the very first day that these bills were given consideration it has been made clear that the only purpose of the debate and of the extension of that debate is to continue to urge that, before these bills are passed, there should be written into the bills, or that there shall be a clear and unequivocal undertaking by the government in relation to its exercise of power under the Electricity and Fluid Exportation Act, that the interests of Canada will first be served, that it will be a Canadian route and that Canadian requirements will be protected for all time in the future before we commit ourselves to an export of power which becomes a vested interest outside Canada which cannot lightly be withdrawn at any future date.
A great deal of concern has been expressed about the possibility that if there is delay gas

and oil may go into the northwest American states from other Canadian sources. We in this parliament represent not only the communities from which we are elected. Collectively, we represent Canada as well; and collectively our interest should at all times be related to that broad concept of the nation which we seek to serve. But let us remember that while we most certainly want to see the legitimate export of oil and gas from Alberta which is consistent with their long-term advantage in that province, we should be much less concerned with the danger of someone else supplying gas in the northwestern United States than we are with the danger of the future requirements of a growing Canada not being met at some time in the distant future.
One of the points to which I referred, and which should be clearly understood in this discussion, is that if we start exporting power it is not like selling so many bushels of wheat, so many tons of coal or so many feet of lumber. When we start to export gas, then communities set up their public services related to the quantity which they receive; and any withdrawal of that gas affects those communities in a manner which could seriously reflect upon our good faith if at some future time we found ourselves forced to withhold from our friendly neighbours that gas which was the basis not only of the building of homes and the provision of services but of the construction of industries which may employ thousands of men. It is in that sense that I speak of it as a vested interest. I do not use the word in any improper manner, in so far as the purpose is concerned. It is an interest which becomes so deeply vested in the users of that gas that we would almost be in the position of being called upon to restrain our own use before we withheld that use from a neighbour to whom we had assured that supply.
In all these discussions we should have before us figures which leave no doubt that any conceivable demand of Canada twenty-five years from now or fifty years from now can be met from our available resources; because power, whether it be electricity, gas or oil, is the most basic and the most fundamental of all raw materials that we possess. We may withdraw nickel, copper or iron from the soil. We may refine it and send it in bulk to the United States, to the United Kingdom or to any other country in the world; and we have received the money for what we have produced. It would be a good thing, of course, if we manufactured the finished product in its final form, in every case. But as to power, we are not only
Alberta Natural Gas Company exporting a commodity, something that comes from the soil; we are exporting the thing which in turn produces products of other kinds. We are exporting the power with which the wheels of industry can be turned and with which the great chemical plants can reduce the coal, the salts and the other resources into the finished products which today have their value in every part of the world. If there is one raw material which we should handle with the utmost care, which we should make sure is going to be preserved for Canadian use first of all and to whatever limit we can use it in an expanding economy, it is power, whether it be electricity, oil or gas.
Since the government must make the decision, since the government must pass on a plan, since the government must have a map, must know what is going to be done both in location and in quantity before the board of transport commissioners can deal with this at all, I submit, Mr. Chairman, that before this house is called upon to vote on bills of this kind the government should take the house into its confidence and fully disclose to us what its plans are, and what responsibility it is going to assume. Anything else is an evasion of that relationship and responsibility to the house about which the house should exercise its own authority no matter to what party any member belongs.
The government is only the executive of this house, and the executive owes it to the members from whom it draws its authority, the members whose confidence it must command, and whose confidence it should be able to command without any mere party adherence, to give to them, and particularly to those who habitually support it, that information which makes them more than rubber stamps in an important case of this kind.
We have been told on a number of occasions that the government itself is greatly anxious to see that hon. members are able to express their opinions; that they should not be denied the opportunity to express their opinions. But hon. members were denied an opportunity to get the information to which they were entitled when this bill was before the committee a short time ago, and hon. members are not being given an opportunity now to express their opinions with any of the knowledge that gives a discussion that exercise of judgment which it should be possible for hon. members to exercise before they give parliamentary authority to these bills.
It is very interesting how personal some of the ministers seem to feel about these bills, which every now and then they claim to be strictly private bills. As will have been noticed from the proceedings that I have read,

Chairman, this is more than a rather simple and forceful exposition of the manner in which the Minister of Trade and Commerce deals so briefly sometimes with the problems of the day. Now, Mr. Chairman, it was an unusual place to suggest that the information should be obtained; but the fact is that if anyone here has access to that particular locality it will ibe the first place anybody has got any real information from, because we have not got it here. I do not know whether the government is waiting for the information to come from that source or not; but most certainly if the government have the information they are not taking the house into their confidence; nor are they taking the people into their confidence, whose interest is the final interest of this parliament and of its executive who serve them with the conveyance of full knowledge to those for whom they act.
That is not where they told you to go, is it?

It is extremely interesting to find that even when the Minister of Trade and Commerce does suggest to hon. members who so slavishly follow him that he knows where to get the information, they are not prepared to follow his advice.
There are three prizes for dumbness, and the hon. member who interrupted gets them all.

These bills deal not merely with the construction of pipe lines, not with just the transmission of gas and oil; they deal with power, from which there could be tremendous development in this country.
When I hear the concern which has been expressed in the house at certain times by those who seem to think they have gained some information from some source other than that mentioned by Mr. Howe, then we find that their concern seems to relate to the fact that we may have a great deal of this power here in Canada.
That same concern was expressed when the new hydroelectric development started in

British Columbia. That same concern was expressed when the hydroelectric development was started in Ontario. That same concern was expressed when the great electrical development took place in the province of Quebec, which has the greatest reserves of electrical energy in Canada. And in every single case what appeared to be unconsumable surpluses have been fully absorbed in the expanding productive capacity of that country.
If the electric energy produced right across this country

in the maritime provinces, and in Quebec, and in Ontario, and in Manitoba and in the prairie provinces, and British Columbia-had been exported to the United States under long-term contracts, we would have found ourselves in a position where we could not easily have withdrawn that power; and we also would have found ourselves in a position where the enormous industries based upon that power would not have been constructed here.
One of the reasons why this country became one of the greatest armourers of the last war was that we had this power available, and because skilled industry had grown up upon the use of that power, with the realization that further power would be available in the years ahead.
Now we are dealing with another type of power, but a type of power which, if it is properly conserved, can be just as important to the future of this country as electricity has been in the past and is in the present. The possibilities in Alberta and British Columbia challenge the imagination of every Canadian who realizes what the possibilities are. If all the oil and gas available in Alberta alone were used for industrial and chemical production here in Canada, always with the hope that there will be gas and oil in Saskatchewan and Manitoba as well, millions of Canadians would find new employment in the years ahead. And upon the basis of that power alone there could be a new population of several millions of people in that part of western Canada.
The figures I am using are in no way an exaggeration. Perhaps it would be well for us to remember that both Ontario and Quebec have more than doubled their population since they started the development of their electrical energy. And what has happened there on the basis of that type of power can happen in Alberta and British Columbia as well. And in many ways there are advantages and opportunities which were not available at that time in Ontario and Quebec. In Alberta and in Manitoba are some of the greatest deposits of coal in the world. This coal is of extremely
Alberta Natural Gas Company high b.t.u. content, although of a sufficiently friable type that in many cases they are regarded as unsuitable for shipment over long distances. I am not saying that that is so; but I do say that that opinion is held in many cases.
But those coals are of the type that can be used for liquefaction and for conversion into all the many chemical and synthetic products which have already been developed in Europe, and were particularly developed in Germany in the years before the war. And if we want one place where our expenditures in research foundations and, in research generally in Canada can find new uses for our resources and new uses for this power, then it is in the application of the discoveries that had already been made in Germany several years ago, and the utilization of our vast coal resources along with this power that is available.
Then, there are minerals, there are clays and there are salts, all of which are waiting to be developed by energetic people, with power of this kind available for industries that can be built. But if we are going to have the kind of industries that can be built, then the thing we have to assure is that there will be not only the basic requirement of power but also an enormous reserve for the future.
If people are going to come in and spend $50 million, $75 million or $100 million on plants-and when I use figures of that kind I am using them with knowledge of investigations that are being conducted right now for the possible use of those resources in that area-if investments of that kind are going to be made, then the thing they have to,be sure of is that as their production develops and new chemical processes emerge from research which, in every case, call for a higher use of power-whatever that power may be- then they must be able to plan 25 or 50 years or more ahead to know that through all that time, and longer, there will always be a surplus of power of that same kind available to them.
Then, in dealing with a subject of this kind, and on that scale, I believe members of this House of Commons, and particularly those on the government side, should say to our executive, to the government, "You have the authority; the board of transport commissioners has no authority or power-"

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as I said before six o'clock, I wish to discuss a matter of great importance to the western farmer, the eastern farmer and feeder, and myself. Two weeks ago, while speaking in the budget debate, I referred to the profit being made by dealers in feed grains in the eastern provinces. Evidently my remarks have been misunderstood, because I have clippings here from the Winnipeg Tribune and the Winnipeg Free Press, and many other papers, commenting on what I said.
The report in the Winnipeg Tribune is much shorter, and is a statement by Mr. Stanley Jones, president of the Winnipeg grain exchange. This newspaper report, which I shall read, is headed "Jones Denies Speculator Hike on Feed Grains." The article goes on to say:
Stanley Jones, president of Winnipeg grain exchange, said Tuesday it is "completely wrong" to blame speculators on the exchange for the high price of feed grain in Ontario.
His statement was issued in reply to a speech in the House of Commons Monday by William Bryce (C.C.F.-Selkirk). Mr. Bryce said there was a difference of $240 a carload last week in the western selling and eastern buying prices for oats. He blamed "speculation."
Mr. Jones said $240 a car is about 12 cents a bushel, and "apparently Mr. Bryce would have it appear that speculators profited to this extent. No. 1 feed oats were quoted by dealers at Toronto last week, on April 18, at $63.14 per ton or $1.07g per bushel, basis delivered most Ontario points. This price is after deduction of freight subsidy rebate of $6 per ton or about 10J cents per bushel. All shippers must buy their supplies from the wheat board, and purchases were made on the Winnipeg grain exchange on that date at 991 cents per bushel in store Fort William. The net cost of delivering to most Ontario points, including balance of freight and loading costs, is 71 cents per bushel. This, added to the purchase price of 991 cents, makes a total cost of $1.061-leaving a possible profit of 1 cents per bushel, or $12.50 per 2,000 bushel car- not $240 as stated by Mr. Bryce. Mr. Bryce should retract his statement since it has no foundation in fact."
I do not need to read the Winnipeg Free Press report as it is similar to that of the Tribune with the exception that it is attributed to the grain trade and not to Mr. Jones. Let me read what I said at page 1813 of Hansard so that I will not be misunderstood any more. I said:
If you compare the amount the western farmer receives for his oats, about $32.35 a ton at the

elevator, and the $76 a ton the hon. member says farmers in his constituency are paying, there is a big difference. To my way of thinking the difference is much too great. I agree that the eastern farmer is paying too much, but I am sure the hon. member will agree that the western producer is not receiving too much. The situation is much the same with respect to barley; but let us deal for a moment with oats, which at last week's prices would cost approximately $59 a ton at Fort William. The freight to points in the vicinity of Montreal or Ottawa would be an additional $2.40. Loading would cost $1.50. Bags would have to be provided, but since they can be used several times, an allowance of $2 per ton for bags should be sufficient. This would give a total of $63.72 per ton at any point in my hon. friend's constituency. Taking the figure at an even $64, when my hon. friend pays $76 the difference is $12 a ton or $480 on a forty-ton car of oats. It would be a good thing if the eastern farmer would check into this and see if someone is not charging more than the traffic should have to bear. On Friday of last week I checked Ottawa prices, and found that wheat, in bags to the farmer, was $74 a ton, oats were $70 and barley was $69. I also checked the Montreal figures and found that wheat was $71, oats $70 and barley $69.
Taking oats again as an example, the price at both Montreal and Ottawa was $70, which, leaves a profit of $6 per ton for the handling of a ton of grain. In other words, on a forty-ton car there would be an allowance of $240 for handling 800 bags of oats, which seems a good profit. I have known dealers in the west who were satisfied to handle oats at 10 cents a bag, and make money. Fluctuations in the market will also cause the dealer to charge the highest price in order to safeguard himself, but if we had steady set prices he could certainly cut down on his margin of profit.
On page 1815 I said:
I started out, Mr. Speaker, to try to show our eastern farmers and feeders that we farmers in the west are not charging them too much for our feed grains. The price is fair and reasonable. I have shown that there is a margin of $240 per car on Montreal and Ottawa prices. Surely grain could be handled more cheaply than that. If the dealers cannot do better than that, I suggest to them that they should set up a co-operative and get service at cost; then if you pay too much for your feed, you will get it back in patronage dividends. That is the solution to the problem; get your co-operative to handle your feed.
In concluding, I want to assure hon. gentlemen who have spoken in this debate on this subject of feed grain prices that the western producer is anxious to have the eastern trade, but he does not like to be accused of charging too much for his grain when that is not the case; and I hope I have proved to them that the producers are not getting too much. Even if the west again increases her hog production, there will always be in the west more feed grains than we can use. We realize that the eastern market is our best outlet for our feed grains, and we do not want to lose it.
At no place have I been discussing speculators' profits. I have been dealing with dealers' profits in eastern Canada. I said that oats to the dealers were costing $63.72. Mr. Jones said oats were $63.14. Therefore there is only 58 cents between his price and my price. His price is cheaper than mine and allows the dealer still more profit. When giving the figures in th'e house I gave the approximate figure of $59 a ton at Fort William. The freight paid by the dealer, $2.40,

and the loading commission, et cetera, would cost $1.50, and then there would be about $2 for bags, making an approximate price of $64 per ton. The grain trade, however, has supplied the actual figures which have been published in the Free Press. They are as follows:

I have nothing to retract, Mr. Speaker. It is unfortunate that Mr. Jones made his statement before he read mine in Hansard, or he would never have made the statement to the paper that he did. When I spoke before I only rose to defend the western farmer. When I heard hon. gentlemen complaining about high prices paid for feed grain, when I heard them blaming the western producer for charging too much, I made inquiries and found that oats were selling at $70 per ton in Ottawa and Montreal. If you take either Mr. Jones' figures or mine, there is still $6 between what the dealer pays and the price at which he sells. If you take a forty-ton car of oats at $6 per ton, you have a profit of $240; you cannot get away from that. The hon. member for Russell (Mr. Gour) quoted a figure at $76 a ton. This would give the dealer $480 for handling a forty-ton car of grain. I said the dealers were taking a greater profit than they should and the western producer was being blamed for the high prices. If there is to be any retraction, Mr. Speaker, I think it should be by Mr. Jones, since no doubt he jumped to the conclusion that, if I were speaking on grain prices, judging from my past record I would be damning the grain speculators on the Winnipeg grain exchange.
When I spoke I only rose to defend the western farmer and show that I thought the dealer was charging too much for the services rendered. I still think $6 per ton or $240 per car is too great a profit, and it is not the fault of the western producer. I made the suggestion previously that the government should conduct an inquiry into the profits of feed dealers. The government is paying this money in subsidizing freight rates to help the 55946-148
Feed Grains
eastern farmer and feeder so he may compete in the world's markets with his pork, poultry, cheese and eggs, and it should be the duty of the government to see that those it is planning to help are not exploited by unscrupulous dealers.
The Winnipeg Free Press came back with another editorial in which they were quite fair to me. They said:
Mr. Bryce strongly repudiated any imputation that he was suggesting western farmers should take less for their oats; his remarks were quite the contrary. He also pointed out that the government freight subsidy on oats meant that the eastern dealers never paid more than $2.40 a ton freight east of Fort William, regardless of where they were landed.
The same editorial contained the solution suggested by the grain trade:
Trade reaction to Mr. Bryce's charges of profiteering by feed dealers retailing to Ontario and Quebec farmers was this:
If the eastern consumer feels he is paying too much for feed grains to the private dealer, he has an obvious recourse-the open market for coarse grains. He can either arrange purchase himself and look after details of shipment, or a broker would be eager to handle the transaction for him at a charge of approximately one-half cent per bushel.
I can assure hon. members that this is not the solution to the problem. We have had that system too long. The system we have now may not be perfect, but it is much better than anything we had before, and I hope we do not go back to the old method.
I want to mention one more thing before I conclude. I have in my hand a clipping from the Stonewall Argus of May 3, 1950. This is a column under the title "The world of wheat" by H. G. L. Strange, and the article is headed "Growing Discontent". It concludes in this way:
The whole matter is becoming complicated by the dissatisfaction of eastern feeders who complain about the high prices they have to pay for coarse grains. Mr. William Bryce, member of parliament, recently asked the government to set up a board to investigate the whole matter of the purchase and sale of western grains.
Nowhere did I ask the government to set up a board to investigate the whole matter of the purchase and sale of western grains. What I did say appears at page 1815 of Hansard:
Perhaps the best thing to do is to have the government check the eastern prices. They are paying $6 to $23.80 per ton subsidy at different points to enable the feeder to get grain at his local point at a reasonable price in order to compete in the production of hogs, poultry and cheese. I am sure that all western farmers will support the eastern farmers in a demand for an inquiry into eastern feed prices. It would clear the air and expose anyone who is taking more profit than he deserves for the services he renders in the feed situation.
I hope I have made clear to hon. members my object in rising this evening. To the grain

Winnipeg Postal Employees exchange people I would say not to jump to conclusions before reading what I really did say.

speechtext:
Just before you leave the chair, Mr. Speaker, there is a matter on which I wish to say a few words. It may seem to some to be a small grievance, but it is the kind of grievance that is most annoying to the people who suffer its consequences. The matter about which I wish to say just a word is set out very clearly in certain answers to questions I placed on the order paper, those questions and answers appearing on page 837 of Hansard for March 16, 1950. They relate to the observance of civic holiday, as far as the postal employees in the city of Winnipeg are concerned.
It so happened that in 1948, for the first time in recent years at any rate, the employees of the post office in Winnipeg were given the day off with pay. They dared to believe that at long last they were being put on the same basis as the employees of the post office here in Ottawa, who for a number of years have had civic holiday as a holiday with pay. But lo and behold, when civic holiday came along in August of 1949, these post office employees in Winnipeg were denied the holiday with pay. Some were given leave to take the day off and although their pay cheques for that month were not decreased as a result, they were made to pay back what they received for that holiday from the overtime they accumulated during the Christmas rush.
On taking up this matter with the Postmaster General (Mr. Rinfret) by correspondence I received an interesting reply, to the effect that the Postmaster General had found it necessary to deny that holiday with pay to those employees in Winnipeg last August by virtue of a directive from the Secretary of State. That led me to ask these questions which appeared on Hansard for March 16, and the answers make it clear that in 1946, 1947, 1948 and 1949 the employees of the post office in Ottawa were given civic holiday as a holiday with pay. Those same answers make it clear that in Winnipeg they did not get it in 1946 or 1947; as I have already pointed out, they got it in 1948 and they thought that at last the discrimination against them was ended, but in 1949 they were again denied that holiday with pay.
It seemed very clear from the answers the Postmaster General had to give to my questions that this was a matter of discrimination. It is not .the most important matter one could raise in this house; just at


the moment the people of Winnipeg are not worrying about holidays, because they are literally in a state of siege and working very hard against the flood waters of the Red river; but it is one of those things that are very annoying.
One of my questions on March 16 looked to the future, and was in these terms:
Have any steps been taken to eliminate discrimination in this matter?
The answer to that question was:
The question is under consideration by the government, and a definite decision will be made prior to the observance of civic holiday next summer.
I have two requests to make in connection with this matter, and the reason I felt it necessary to raise this before Your Honour leaves the chair, although we are going to deal with post office matters when we get into the committee of supply, is the fact that it has been made clear that the Acting Postmaster General (Mr. Lapointe) is going to deal almost exclusively with this question of the denial of the use of the mails to certain people. The two points that I have raised before by letter, without yet getting satisfaction, and the two that I now repeat, are quite simple: In the first place, I feel that these employees are justified in asking that the situation of last August be rectified, and that they be compensated for the day that they were forced to work last August, in lieu of not receiving the holiday as did their fellow post office employees in the city of Ottawa. The same request applies in the case of those who had the day off but had to make up for it at Christmas.
The other request is in terms of the future. I urge the government to make a decision soon, and to announce it as early as possible, as to what the policy will be with respect to civic holiday this year, and in future years. Surely, if it is possible to grant the civic holiday as a holiday with pay to post office employees, and other civil service employees, here in the city of Ottawa, and I think it should be, it is only fair that the same holiday with pay should be granted in other cities where civic holiday is declared for that city as a whole. I dare to believe from the answer that was given to me that that consideration may result in favourable action so far as the future is concerned. I hope so, and I hope the announcement will be made soon. But I want to say to the Acting Postmaster General and through him to the Postmaster General that the employees concerned will not be satisfied unless there is also a rectification of the discrimination against them in connection with Hvic holiday last August.
