speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the matter of the protection of the mails from being used for schemes devised or intended to deceive the public is one of considerable importance. From one standpoint it affects certain rights of individual brokers, and of course no government wishes to deal unfairly with them. From another standpoint it affects the efficient workings of a free society; for I submit, sir, it is important to a free society that the integrity of its methods in raising risk capital for the development of its natural resources should be protected from any corruption by fraud.
Not only the Roman law but every civilized law that has yet appeared in history has set forth a conception of property as being a natural right, and not a mere concession of the state. That being so, one of the most important functions of the law is to promote diffusion of property. Such diffusion is one of the most effective bulwarks of free society. The law, therefore, should be used for the protection of the small investor, who on the one hand can ill afford to lose his capital, but on the other, because he usually lacks both the breadth of investment experience and expert advice, is so often fair game for the unscrupulous.
Moreover, another aspect of this matter is that the unsurpassed reputation of Canada throughout the world for honesty and fair dealing, which has been so dearly purchased by us through long years of honourable conduct on the part of Canadian citizens, should not be besmirched or impaired by a few people for selfish and dishonest reasons. Therefore, when the member for Eglinton raised the question in the house as to the propriety and the validity of the postal regulation which had been made by the Postmaster General, he raised a matter which is a serious one, and which deserves careful and serious consideration.
Unfortunately at that time, as I then indicated to the house, the general counsel for the Broker Dealers Association had just written a letter to me dealing with these 55946-148a
Supply-Post Office
postal regulations, and which I had not had the opportunity to consider. The suggestion was made that on the next occasion on which we went into committee of supply a careful examination of the remarks both of the leader of the opposition and of the member for Eglinton, but more especially of the considered representations in writing of the general counsel for the Broker Dealers Association, would be placed before the members. I think that, because the statement made by Mr. McTague in the form of a letter addressed to me as the Minister of Justice is a considered, careful statement of the whole position of the broker dealers, and on that account is perhaps a little more thorough than mere extemporaneous efforts could be, the fair way to deal with these representations and to lay this matter before the members is to read the first points which Mr. McTague makes in this letter, and then read the reply to the first point, and so on. In that way we could dispose of the matter. Then I would hope that, if time permitted, I might deal finally with some of the observations made by the leader of the opposition and the member for Eglinton.
The letter from Mr. McTague is dated 220 Bay street, Toronto, April 26, 1950. The first point has had fairly lengthy treatment, and he starts it in this way:
As counsel for the Broker Dealers Association of Ontario and acting only in that capacity and not for any individuals concerned, I wish to put before you certain submissions with respect to the action of the Post Office Department stopping the mails to people in, or remotely associated with, the security business here in Toronto.
In the first place, my submission is that under the rule of law, to which we lawyers continually pay lip service, the procedure followed in the Post Office Department is totally without justification.
The powers of the post office generally in so far as they appear to be relevant to the matter alleged to be involved here are, I think, to be found in the Post Office Act, section 7 (d), permitting the making of regulations-
He sets out the whole section, but I shall just refer to those matters which are relevant to the subject under discussion.
-regulations "for marking on the covering of letters, circulars or other mailable matters suspected to concern illegal lotteries, etc. . . or concerning schemes devised or intended to deceive or defraud the public, for the purpose of obtaining money under false pretences, whether such letters, circulars or other mailable matter are addressed to or received by mail from places within or without Canada, a warning that they are suspected to be of a fraudulent character, and for returning such letters, circulars and other mailable matter to the senders".
In other words, Mr. Chairman, that is the statutory authority for two regulations, Nos.

Supply-Post Office
204 and 206, which Mr. McTague proceeds to set out in his letter in another paragraph commencing as follows:
The relevant regulations pursuant to section 7 (d) appear to be 204 and 206, reading as follows:
I shall not bother to read No. 204 in full, although I hope with the approval of members that Mr. McTague's letter to me of April 17, 1950, might be published in Hansard, as an appendix, along with my reply to Mr. McTague dated May 2.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order. Has the Minister of Justice the unanimous consent of the committee to put on Hansard as an appendix the letters to which he has referred?

Agreed. .
(For text of letters, see appendix, pages 2347-49.)

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Regulation 206 reads as follows:
The Postmaster General has power, under the statute, to mark or cause to be marked upon the covers of letters, circulars, or other mail matter suspected to concern schemes devised or intended to deceive or defraud the public for the purpose *of obtaining money under false pretences, whether such letters, circulars or other mail matter are addressed to or received by mail from places within or without Canada, "suspected to be of a fraudulent character", and to return such letters, circulars or other mail matter to the senders.
I might interject again that the so-called orders complained of here consist of actions taken to mark these mail matters and return them to the senders under this regulation 204 passed pursuant to section 7 (d) of the act.
You mean regulation 206.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Yes, regulation 206. My hon. friend is quite right. Then Hon. Mr. McTague goes on:
I think you will agree that it is trite law that the regulations cannot be extended beyond the authority given in the statute to make them. For the purpose of my submission to you I am not arguing that these regulations go beyond the statutory authority for them, but I do submit as strongly as I can that the deputy Postmaster General has gone far beyond what is provided for in the regulations or the statute in the most arbitrary way.
Without any warning whatever, and on the strength of representations made by the United States Post Office Department at the behest of the United States Securities and Exchange Commission and entirely ex parte, without the persons suspected having an opportunity to be heard, the mails have not only been arbitrarily cut off, but have been required to be forwarded to Ottawa where they are held for an indefinite period without any commitment or statement of intention to prefer any charges in the courts. Not only that, but in separate hearings of aggrieved persons before the deputy Postmaster General, their mail has been released upon the exaction of undertakings that they will not further deal in specified securities, or that they will agree to modify the language and

terms of circulars sent in the future. The whole procedure is in substance a conviction by the deputy Postmaster General without a hearing, punishment by cutting off the mails and the exaction of undertakings as a condition on which the penalty will be suspended.
If there is anything in the Post Office Act justifying such procedure, I am unable to locate it. In addition to that, I cannot conceive of any government putting forward legislation to justify such action by way of amendment to the Post Office Act, and I cannot conceive of any parliament enacting such legislation if it were put forward.
That is Hon. Mr. McTague's first point upon behalf of his client. The answer to this point is as follows:
I have your letter oi April 17 with reference to the action of the post office in stopping the mails of certain brokers. You are acting as counsel for the Broker Dealers Association and not on behalf of any of the persons against whom the "stop" order was directed.
I have inquired as to what took place. The order, which was made with the approval of the Postmaster General and therefore may be regarded as made by him, was to the effect that all mails addressed to or coming from the above (persons named) are to be intercepted and sent specially by first mail to the administration branch, Ottawa. It was stated that this action was being taken as a result of evidence received indicating that the mails were being used for the purpose of obtaining money under false pretences. I am informed that contrary to what you state in your letter the order. was not made at the behest of the United States Securities and Exchange Commission.
The action was taken under the authority of paragraph (d) of section 7 of the Post Office Act which authorizes the Postmaster General to make regulations "for marking on the covering of letters, circulars or other mailable matter suspected to concern" . . .
Then I go on and repeat the provisions of that subsection, and I indicate that "the mailable matter is marked 'nontransmissible' instead of with a warning that it was suspected to be "of a fraudulent character". I continue:
This marking was regarded as less injurious. The matter is returned to the sender.
My information is that each of the brokers named in the order was engaged in the sale of the securities of a single company. The "stop" order was made only after a careful examination was made by experienced officials of the literature which these brokers were circulating, making claims which were so extravagant and untrue as to raise a reasonable suspicion in the mind of the Postmaster General that they related to schemes intended to deceive or defraud the public, for the purpose of obtaining money under false pretences.
Will the minister permit a question?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes, surely.
He refers to experienced officials. Were those officials of the Post Office Department or officials of the justice department?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: They were not of the justice department.
There was no reference in that matter to the justice department for an opinion as to whether there might be any question of deceit?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
No. That is quite right.
Then my letter to Mr. McTague goes on:
I cannot discover any illegality in this procedure. The statute calls on the Postmaster General to refuse the use of the mails to persons whom he reasonably suspects of using the post office facilities to defraud the public. The only question is whether the Postmaster General had reasonable grounds for his suspicion. From the facts when they are disclosed I think you will have to agree that the Postmaster General did have good grounds for his suspicion.
And at the conclusion of my remarks tonight the Acting Postmaster General (Mr. Lapointe) will give some of those grounds in certain cases to members of the committee in order that they may judge as to whether there were any reasonable grounds for suspicion.
The second point which Mr. McTague makes starts out in this way:
Mr. Turnbull-
That is the deputy postmaster general.
-seems to take undue comfort, in my opinion, in the Literary Publications case, I think it is, in British Columbia (58 C. C. C. 385), in giving him the right to do anything and considering that whatever he does is not reviewable by the courts. He does not seem to realize that the court in that case simply held that there was a right to exercise a discretion under the statute and the discretion having been duly and properly exercised, the courts would not review it. That case concerned an action for damages following an acquittal after a prosecution under the Criminal Code. It appears to me to be no authority for the proposition that the Post Office Department can legislate through the process of administration and in fact set up what amounts to a star chamber. I recall hearing a careful speech made by yourself on the rule of law with many references to the admonitions of Coke to King James. In this affair it is McTague humbly putting forward the same type of admonition to Turnbull through your good self as an understanding intermediary, I hope.
Who is writing this?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Mr. McTague.
To you?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Yes. He goes on:
There just cannot be two standards of fraud, one laid down by the courts and a different and private one by the Post Office Department. The Post Office Department has not, as yet, attained judicial status. It appears by its recent actions merely to assert that very untenable position.
The answer to that point is as follows:
Perhaps it should be remarked in this connection-
I say to Mr. McTague in my letter.
-that none of the brokers has seen fit to take action against the Postmaster General alleging wrongful action on his part, a remedy which the court of
Supply-Post Office
appeal of British Columbia held, in the case of Literary Recreations Limited v. Sauve C. C. C. page 358, to be open to a person against whom such an order has been made.
In other words, in the very case which Mr. McTague is quoting in his letter it was indicated that persons offended by a wrongful order had a right of action against the Postmaster General. My letter to Mr. McTague continues:	.
The next point made by you is that the post office cannot "legislate through the process of administration and in fact set up what amounts to a star chamber."
Who is saying this? Is that you?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I am saying this to Mr. McTague:
I am afraid I do not follow this contention since it appears to me that the Postmaster General was doing precisely what the statute authorized and required him to do.
Mr. McTague's third point is this, and I quote from his letter:
As you know, I have had a rather wide experience in the security business.
And he is quite right in saying that. Mr. McTague was one of the most distinguished security commissioners that the province of Ontario ever had. He continues:
It is my opinion, and I have comparatively recently put my opinion in writing for the benefit of the United States securities and exchange commission, that no provincial legislature has power to control or regulate international or interprovincial trade in securities. While I know of no case directly dealing with securities on the proposition, it has been laid down in reference to other commodities more than once that there is no such power in the province. I make* brief reference to the Natural Products Marketing Board case in British Columbia.
On this third point I replied in my letter as follows:
You point out that the province has no power to control or regulate international trade in securities. That is certainly true where the post office is the medium used for carrying on the international trade in securities. But I suggest that it follows from your statement that in this case the Postmaster General is the proper official and the only official who is legally qualified to exercise such control under section 7, subsection (d), of the Post Office Act.
The fourth point of Mr. McTague's letter is stated in these words:
The only jurisdiction which can validly enact legislation to control and regulate the sale of securities internationally and interprovincially is the Canadian parliament. If the policy of enacting such legislation is determined upon the government can readily put forward a statute and take its responsibility in that regard. If it does not care to accept such responsibility, surely it should not permit or even tolerate the setting up of a securities commission de facto, but certainly not de jure under the present act within the Post Office Department. Yet that is exactly what is being done at the present time.

Supply-Post Office
My answer to this fourth point is as follows:
You contend that parliament has not set up a "securities commission de facto" within the Post Office Department. I entirely agree with this contention. The Postmaster General's job is not to operate a securities commission. The Postmaster General's duty is to see that the post office facilities are not used to defraud the public. While his efforts to this end may result in protecting investors against the purchase of fraudulent securities, this result is purely consequential and is not, primarily, his responsibility. Under the law, his statutory duty and responsibility is to maintain the efficiency and reputation of the postal services which he directs. It is for this purpose that he is empowered to stop mail which he suspects is being posted for fraudulent purposes.
Mr. McTague's fifth point is as follows:
At this time there is no law in Canada prohibiting the sale of securities in the United States by circular or otherwise. If the circular is considered to be fraudulent under the laws of Canada let prosecution be brought in the criminal courts, but let us still maintain the fundamental principle of the rule of law and once again abolish star chamber methods from which already too many innocent people have suffered greatly.
To stop the mails and ruin people in business on the evidence of circulars, telephone conversations and other gossip, which have taken place many months ago, seems to me a most extraordinary procedure.
I am forwarding a copy of this letter to the Right Honourable the Prime Minister and of course also to Mr. Turnbull.
The answer to this fifth and last point, as set out in my letter to Mr. McTague, is as follows:
As to the question whether criminal proceedings should be instituted, it is not the Postmaster General's duty to prosecute persons guilty of criminal offences. I do not need to remind you that it is the attorney general of the province who enforces the criminal law. The Postmaster General's duty is to take appropriate actions where he has reasonable grounds for suspecting that the mails are being used for fraudulent purposes.
In conclusion, I think I should say that where the state operates a public utility such as the post office, a railway or a radio station there is not thereby conferred upon each citizen an absolute right to utilize the utility, but a conditional right only, the condition being that there should be no abuse. The utility must be operated strictly for the public benefit. The government officials operating the same should have at least as wide powers to protect the public against abuse as the private owners of a public utility would have to protect their patrons. In the case of the post office, parliament has seen fit, in order to protect the service against abuse, to authorize the Postmaster General to refuse the use of mails if he has reasonable grounds for suspecting that a person is making an improper and fraudulent use of them. I am informed that this provision is one of long standing having been introduced in the act by Sir John A. Macdonald in 1889; that it has been beneficially invoked' hundreds of times throughout the intervening years; and that similar provisions will be found in the post office statutes of other free countries.
Notwithstanding these facts, the government is quite open-minded with regard to this section and the powers created under it. For many months before this order was made, the government had been engaged in preparing the first general revision and consolidation of the Post Office Act since 1922.
	'
In this connection, it has been giving special attention to sections such as section 7 (d) which vest rather wide powers in the Postmaster General. We are inclined to think from the consideration which we have given this matter so far that the experience of our own post office and the post offices of other free countries over the years indicates that the power under section 7 (d) should be retained. We are also inclined to think, however, that it might perhaps be advisable that a summary appeal should be provided from the order of the Postmaster General to the courts; and that upon the hearing of this appeal the appellant should have the right to adduce any relevant evidence in addition to that upon which the Postmaster General based his order. The appellate tribunal should have power either to confirm or discharge the order of the Postmaster General. Pending the hearing and disposition of such appeal, however, the Postmaster General's order should remain in effect and should also, of course, remain in effect if confirmed by the court appealed to.
We can well understand that the organization which you represent will have well-informed views upon this subject matter and if it wishes to present a brief on any of the matters under the Post Office Act in which it has an interest, I can assure you that the government will be glad indeed to give its representations the most careful and thorough consideration.
Now, so much for the points raised in a careful and systematic manner by Mr. McTague. I might spend a little time now upon the points raised by hon. members in this house.
Dealing first of all with the remarks of the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) on April 15 last, as set out at page 1562 of Hansard, where he is reported as saying this:
I wish to ask the Minister of Justice whether he has given consideration to the extent to which the Post Office Department is usurping the authority and responsibilities of the Department of Justice in acting as a court by making decisions as to the guilt or otherwise of certain people using the mails of Canada.
Now, I am not too clear as to the precise point the hon. member is making in that language, but I think I can answer all possible meanings that could be given to it by making two or three simple statements of fact.
In the first place I would point out that the Postmaster General cannot in this case be usurping the authority of the Minister of Justice, since the powers which are invoked here in this case are clearly those which the act vests in the Postmaster General and not in the Minister of Justice. And therefore in using those powers, whatever he is doing he cannot possibly be usurping the functions of the Minister of Justice.
Then, secondly, I point out that neither the Department of Justice nor the Post Office Department has the authority or the responsibility to act as a court, either by making decisions as to the guilt or otherwise of certain people using the mails of Canada or, indeed, in any other way.

Thirdly, I would point out, repeating what has already been said, that in connection with the postal orders under discussion and under criticism by the opposition it is the statutory duty of the Postmaster General, pursuant to section 7(d), where he considers that there are reasonable grounds lor suspecting that mail matter coming under his charge concerns a scheme intended to defraud the public and is being sent through the mails, to make these orders that are under attack.
In this connection, I do not think it can be emphasized too strongly-having regard to the reference by the leader of the opposition to courts, and to other suggestions which were made that these people should be prosecuted- it cannot be emphasized too strongly that the Postmaster General decides nothing as to the guilt or innocence of these persons. He decides only whether or not there is reasonable ground for his suspicion that the postal service is being wrongfully used. And if he suspects upon reasonable grounds that the postal service is being wrongfully used, then he has the power to make these orders which are under debate.
Suggestions have been made, notably by the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming), that the Postmaster General, in acting as he did, usurped-I do not know whether that is the word the hon. member used; in fact I do not think he did use that word, but his meaning was clear-that the Postmaster General in making these orders was usurping or interfering with the functions of the securities commissioner of the province. The hon. member put it this way at page 1638 of Hansard:
We have laws to deal with such cases. We have the Criminal Code, and, as to the rights between broker and client and the measure of responsibility that those engaged in the purchase and sale of stocks owe to the public, we have in all provinces- we certainly have in Ontario-securities laws and securities officials. This case may be, and no doubt is, one for the securities commission of the province of Ontario, which has ample power to deal with brokers who are carrying on their business in violation of the law without due regard for honesty in business dealings.
Whose statement is that?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
It is the statement made by the hon. member for Eglinton in this house. This statement continues:
Therefore in my submission it is not necessary for the Post Office Department to undertake to make laws in substitution for the Criminal Code of Canada as enacted by this parliament, and in substitution for the laws of the province in relation to regulation of transactions involved in the purchase and sale of stocks and the control and regulation of the activities of those engaged in that business.
Supply-Post Office
This argument, as I shall show, is quite incorrect. I have already shown that the Postmaster General has the undoubted power under the Post Office Act to make orders such as those under discussion. I submit that the exercise by the Postmaster General of such powers as those under the Post Office Act is no interference at all with the authority of the provincial securities commission. Indeed, it is the discharge of a completely separate and distinct duty.
In discharging his duties the Postmaster General is not bound by the decisions of any provincial securities commission, nor does the law permit him to abrogate his responsibilities and functions in favour of a provincial securities commission, because it is a well established fact and principle, with which I am sure the hon. member for Eglinton would be the first to agree, that in exercising discretionary power an administrative officer must make his own decision and must not accept the decision of another person. The Postmaster General of course may have recourse to the provincial securities commission or to any other reliable source for materials upon which to make up his mind; but so far as the actual making up of his mind is concerned, he must do it quite independently of any provincial commissioner or of any other source of information that he may have.
And, sir, the point upon which he has to make up his mind is not as to whether or not the dealer should be licensed, nor as to whether or not trading in a certain stock or other security should be permitted. The point which the Postmaster General must decide is the simple one of whether or not there are good grounds for suspecting that postal privileges under the Postmaster General are being abused.
The second point in this connection I should like to make is that, quite unlike the provincial securities commission, the Postmaster General is not in any way concerned about the intrinsic value of the security that is being dealt in, except in so far as that intrinsic value of the security may create in his mind a legitimate and well-founded suspicion that the mails are being used to defraud. The Postmaster General's only duty is to concern himself with false and fraudulent representations made through the mails in respect of the sale of the security.
I think I should emphasize in this connection that while the provincial securities commission-and I am sure the hon. member for Eglinton knows about this, and will agree with it-license the dealer and approve of the security, and pass upon the prospectus, the provincial securities commission does not

Supply-Post Office
ordinarily or necessarily pass upon or even see a great deal of the advertising and sales literature put out by the brokers. They do not necessarily know whether that sales literature is true or false, objectionable or otherwise.
Moreover, as the Hon. Mr. McTague points out in his letter, one of the great problems of any provincial securities commission- and especially in cases such as we are discussing here, which involve the sale of Canadian securities internationally, in to the United States-the great problem of a provincial securities commission in respect of such traffic is that it has, according to Mr. McTague, who should know, and who is an expert in the field, no power whatever to control or regulate international or interprovincial trade in securities. Therefore when the hon. member for Eglinton says, "We certainly have in Ontario securities laws and securities officials, and this case may be and no doubt is one for the securities commission of the province of Ontario, which has ample power to deal with brokers who are carrying on their business in violation of the law", he is making a statement that is quite incorrect. It is incorrect because most of the transactions upon the basis of which the Postmaster General made the orders which are under debate, and under criticism by my hon. friend, concern interprovincial and international trade in stocks. As to this trade-and I am sure my hon. friend will agree with me upon reflection-the provincial securities commissions do not exercise any authority for the excellent reason that they have no power to do so. Their powers are intraprovincial powers. Moreover, not only have they no power to do so but the provincial legislatures have no constitutional authority, according to Mr. McTague, to clothe provincial securities commissioners with such power.
Thus, if these powers which the Postmaster General has invoked in the present case are not used in proper cases, which we contend the present ones to be, to prevent the misuse of the mails in interprovincial and international trade in stocks, there are no provincial powers of any kind that can be invoked to prevent such misuse. Thus, far from the Postmaster General having overridden or ignored the authority of the provincial securities commissions or invaded the field of provincial rights, as seemed to be implied by the remarks made by members of the opposition, the Postmaster General has instead merely prevented the misuse of the post office, which is his responsibility. In the cases which we are considering he has done this, for the most part, in cases with which,

according to the Hon. Mr. McTague, neither the provincial securities commissions nor the provincial legislatures had power to deal.
Let us say some of the cases.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
My hon. friend, the Acting Postmaster General, can speak more accurately on that point than I can. I doubt, however, if there are any purely intraprovincial cases, but I am merely dealing with the law. The Acting Postmaster General will deal with the facts. I think I should add, lest there be any misunderstanding, that no one should infer from what I have just said that the Postmaster General has not power, in relation to the use of the mails for the sale of stocks wholly within any province, to make such an order as we are now discussing. He has that power also, but there is the difference that in most of the cases we are discussing he has the power to make this order in respect of trafficking in stocks internationally and interprovincially, which is beyond the jurisdiction of the provincial securities commissions.
That comprises all the legal points which arise in this connection. My hon. friend, the Acting Postmaster General, will outline the facts upon which some of these orders were based in order to give hon. members information as to whether there were reasonable grounds for the exercise of the Postmaster General's discretion.

Mr. Chairman, my colleague the Minister of Justice has set forth the legal position in this matter of fraud orders issued against certain corporations and individuals. His statement to the house clearly establishes that the Postmaster General is empowered to prevent the mails from being used for fraudulent purposes. To this power given the Postmaster General by parliament there is a corresponding duty to prevent His Majesty's mails from being used as an instrument of fraud. The intention of parliament to protect His Majesty's mails in this regard was so definite that the Postmaster General is empowered to take the necessary preventive action when he has justifiable and reasonable grounds to suspect that the mails are being used to perpetrate fraud.
Therefore, in my estimation the point at issue is: Was the Postmaster General justified in taking action as he did in the specific cases which are before us and which are being discussed tonight? If I may, Mr. Chairman, I should like to dispose immediately of the imputation that the action of the Postmaster General of Canada was taken solely at the behest of United States authorities, and was based otherwise only on a few circulars, rumours and gossip generally in

the brokerage field. As the bulk of the circulars in question were addressed to citizens of the United States it was only natural that the majority of the complaints received came from United States citizens. I feel sure it will be conceded that they had a right to protest against questionable actions by Canadian citizens or by persons operating in Canada just as I am sure that the Postmaster General had not only the right but also the clear duty to take appropriate action.
I want to emphasize that we did not issue fraud orders at the behest of the United States government or of its officials. Nor did we take the word of United States authorities as to these transactions about which complaints had been received. We obtained affidavits together with circulars and other material. We went further than that. Appropriate inquiries were made, investigations were carried out and expert advice was sought. I can assure hon. members who are interested in this matter that in every case the Postmaster General had good and sufficient reasons for believing that the mails were being used for fraudulent purposes.
May I ask a question? When the Acting Postmaster General says that expert advice was sought will he indicate the nature of the expert advice to which he refers?

If the leader of the opposition will permit me to carry on with my statement, which is quite short, I think he will find the answer to his question. It is not my intention, Mr. Chairman, to analyse tonight every single case where prohibitory orders have been issued, but I believe it would be useful to outline some of the methods used, and to quote from some of the literature issued. I have here the -case of one company dealing in oil stocks, and using the services of a broker. Circulars issued by this broker-dealer and distributed by mail included the following statements:
This company holds leases on a quarter section in the Redwater Bruederheim area between acreage held by Imperial Oil. In addition, the company holds fifteen well sites in the Lloydminster field, which has been growing at a phenomenal rate in the past two years. Since the astounding results at Leduc, Lloydminster and Redwater-and I'm convinced that the holdings of-
This particular company.
-hold the promise of profits and fortune such as we have often dreamed about and hope to share.
Again I quiite:
This I believe is one of the greatest chances at a fortune that has ever been offered to you. Here, I believe, is your chance to make $25 grow to $1,000 55946-149
Supply-Post Office
-$250 grow to $10,000. Only now are the tremendous possibilities being realized-and we are getting in at the right time.
The dealer continues:
In my last letter I told you that the experts estimate Redwater's recoverable oil reserves at 30,000 barrels per acre. As the holdings of this company in the Redwater-Bruederheim area comprise a quarter section (160 acres) that's sufficient to drill four wells, which, assuming comparable results, would work out to a potential of 4,800,000 barrels of oil. At the current wellhead price of $2.68 per barrel, the gross money value on this basis would be $12,864,000.
Competent authorities of the government of Alberta, in which this property is situated, state that instead of this material being called literature it should be called sucker bait, as the property of this company is strictly wildcat and is unproven. The suspicion of fraud lies in the extravagant and misleading claims. Although the literature refers to the Redwater area, the company has no property in that rich field but only in the Bruederheim or Lloydminster area. To talk about the Redwater-Bruederheim area, again according to the testimony of these officials, is sheer nonsense; and the holdings of this company in the Lloydminster area hold even less than a gambler's chance of rich reward.
These again are not the statements or opinions of the Postmaster General or of his officials; they are the recorded views of responsible officials of the Alberta government. The implication that the acreage is in the Redwater field is misleading, and is suspected of being intended to deceive. The information given in these circulars and letters shipped by the broker-dealer is not in accordance with fact. These are the grounds on which, in this case, the Postmaster General reasonably believed that the mails were being used with intent to deceive and defraud.
I have another case here, Mr. Chairman, of another company selling oil stocks in Alberta, using the services of two brokerage firms. The circulars issued in regard to this company by implication endeavour to link the properties with those of producing properties in the Leduc oil field. Statements are made with the intent of making believe that the wells drilled in this area are successful, to greatly enhance the company's assets. A few of the statements made concerning the possibilities of this- company are as follows:
There appears little or no doubt that all of the sixteen wells scheduled for this quarter section will be commercial producers.
The company has every expectation of being able to look forward within the near future to eighteen producing oil wells.
Although No. 5 well has been delayed, it is only a few feet from No. 3 producer and there is virtually no doubt that it will be equally successful.

Supply-Post Office
The large amount of proven oil reserves below each of these wells has greatly enhanced the company's asset position.
Today these shares are backed not by just a few acres of grazing land but by ten successfully drilled wells of which three are producers and the others are to be put into production as soon as possible-over ten thousand acres-fifteen square miles-of potentially rich oil leases and reservations.
Thus you can see that no longer is this company a "chance" or a speculation.
Many other similar statements could be quoted. So much for the claims; what are the facts? All the rights in one of the fields exploited by this company are rank wildcat. No wells have ever been started near this acreage. The company has drilled a few dry or duster wells in the Lloydminster area. Some of the other wells are not commercially successful. Others have produced water when pumped, are worthless and must be abandoned. The three wells which are producing are pumped; that is, the oil does not flow but has to be pumped. The broker-dealer exploits this information by giving it an improper twist in order to mislead his clients. He indicates that the pumps are to control the flow, whereas in fact such wells as this company has producing do not flow; they must be pumped to get the oil, not to control it.
Again, the foregoing are not the statements of the Postmaster General or of his officials; they are the recorded views of impartial, competent and reliable officials of the Alberta government. The Postmaster General, I think, was justified in concluding that the mails were being used with intent to deceive or to obtain money under false pretences, and in acting accordingly. There again I think the facts speak for themselves.
Another gentleman who had his licence to operate as a broker cancelled by the Ontario securities commission continued to promote his own enterprises, selling his own stock direct instead of through a broker. This is the gentleman, incidentally, who forfeited $50,000 bail in the United States. Not at all abashed by the reasons which prevented him from acting as broker, he has made a great virtue out of necessity and now proudly proclaims in his literature that he employs no brokers and therefore all the money goes to the development of the property.
I believe, Mr. Chairman, that the few examples I have cited are sufficient to .establish the unquestionable right of the Postmaster General to conclude that the mails were being used for schemes and devices intended to deceive or defraud the public. In some cases certain individuals may have been used as fronts for the real transgressors, but the fact that they were associated with the offending

concerns and allowed their names to be used in the literature made it necessary to include them in the prohibitory order.
Much has been said about the Postmaster General usurping the rights and functions of the securities commission of Ontario. I believe this point was dealt with satisfactorily by my colleague, the Minister of Justice; but, as he pointed out, with the best intentions in the world the securities commission of Ontario could not act in these cases because it lacked jurisdiction. That does not mean, however, that it has not been aware of what has been going on, and has not regretted this situation. It is interesting to note what the commission, through its chairman, had to say on this matter in a report dated February 3 of this year:
It is not necessary to labour the fact that all aspects of trading outside the province have been a grave concern over a period of years since certain promotional houses have been financially able to use the mails extensively in soliciting inquiries or subscriptions for securities.
He adds:
In my view these facts afford a glaring example of over-reaching. They further demonstrate that dealers may readily resort to tactics outside Ontario as suggested in the notice of September 6. 1949, which they would not consider employing in Ontario where chances of detection would be much greater.
Before I conclude, Mr. Chairman, there is one point I wish to touch upon, and that concerns some of the remarks made by the member for Eglinton to the effect that a statement was made by the deputy postmaster general that he did not care what the Supreme Court of Canada, or any other court, might say about the matter. In other words, that power was given to him under the act and the regulations, and h would use those powers without the slightest regard for what the courts might say. This, Mr. Chairman, is a serious accusation. I have looked carefully into the matter, and find that the alleged statement is incorrect. At no time did the deputy postmaster general say anything of the kind. He is well aware that the power under the act is given to the Postmaster General, not to the deputy postmaster general. He placed all the relevant facts before the Postmaster General, who authorized the issuance of these prohibitory orders. All that has been said on this subject by anyone connected with the Post Office Department, from the minister down, is what has been pointed out here tonight, namely, that the law gives the Postmaster General the power to act, and that his right to do so has been upheld by the court, including the supreme court of British Columbia. To twist that statement into an assertion that the deputy postmaster general does not care what the courts might say is a misrepresentation made to the hon.

gentleman, which I have no doubt he accepted in good faith, but which he repeated without too much regard for his responsibility.
I now come, Mr. Chairman, to a statement made by the leader of the opposition on April 5, to the effect that the action taken had the effect of preventing the receipt by some people of securities and other documents to which they were entitled. I have no doubt that here again such information was given to the leader of the opposition, and that he accepted it in good faith, but that is not the case, Mr. Chairman. In every case where the companies represented that they had certificates to deliver for shares or securities bought and paid for, they were permitted to mail out such certificates. It would seem that some hon. members who are so deeply concerned in this matter are constantly trying to create the impression that some law is being flouted by the Post Office Department. In his statement the leader of the opposition used the words of the Globe and Mail I believe, and stated that the post office had set itself up as a court, presumably in defiance of the law. Let me again point out, Mr. Chairman, what has been made clear, that the law giving the Postmaster General power to act is explicit and unassailable. It confers on the Postmaster General not only the right but the responsibility to make sure that the post office facilities are not used as instruments of fraud. It has been on the statute books for more than sixty years, during which time it has been invoked repeatedly to prevent the perpetration of fraud and the irregular use of the mails.
It may be that the great majority of the members have never been aware of the existence of this section of the statute, and the regulations enacted thereunder. Certainly some of the remarks in this house, and some of the comments in the press, would indicate that many people were not aware of the exact purpose of this legislation which, in the words of Sir John Macdonald under whose government it was passed in 1889 as my colleague the Minister of Justice mentioned, was intended to give the Post Office Department the power to determine what was and was not deemed desirable under this act, and to prohibit the circulation of dangerous and improper articles. May I say that, in the light of such experience as I have so far been able to acquire, I am inclined to believe that the statutory power and the broad authorization given to the Postmaster General, as previously explained, may still be considered necessary when the taking of immediate action is of essential importance for the protection of the public. It is only fair, however, that the aggrieved party should 55946-149J
Supply-Post Office
be given the opportunity of submitting expeditiously reasons why the order complained of should not be maintained. For the present, and at least until some more effective means have been found of protecting His Majesty's mails from being used against the public interest, I submit, Mr. Chairman, that this parliament and the public of Canada should hesitate to cast aside this old statutory provision which has rendered such excellent service in the past.

A statement has been made on the calling of the first item for the Post Office Department by the two ministers. You have seen us report progress on the first item and then continue at another sitting. I do not see how the gentleman-
Why should this not be discussed now?
Without developing any heat on this, Mr. Chairman,-
Oh, oh.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO CONVEYANCE, LEASES, DEFENCE LANDS, ETC.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO CONVEYANCE, LEASES, DEFENCE LANDS, ETC.
speechtext:
By this bill it is proposed to revise and combine the provisions of two existing statutes, namely, the Public Lands Grants Act and the Ordnance and Admiralty Lands Act. The purpose of this revision is to bring these laws up to date, to drop sections which have become obsolete and to consolidate the remaining provisions into one measure. In addition, several sections of the Dominion Lands Act are embodied in this proposed consolidation. Other sections of the Dominion Lands Act are included in the territorial lands bill. Upon the passing of that bill the Dominion Lands Act will be repealed.
The Public Lands Grants Act as it now exists is in the nature of a residuary measure granting power to the governor in council to
Public Lands Grants Act dispose of or deal with lands for which no other authority exists. The three main sections of the present Public Lands Grants Act have been carried into the proposed new act. These three sections deal with (1) the use of words of limitation in crown grants; (2) powers of the governor in council; and (3) authority for the execution of leases.
The first of these sections is broadened; as it presently stands, this section applies only to the provinces of Ontario, Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta, the Northwest Territories and Yukon Territory. The purpose of the amendment is to make the sections applicable to all provinces that have abolished words of limitation.
The second section gives the governor in council power to make regulations for the disposal of lands, to prescribe a tariff of fees and to fix a rate of interest to be charged on rent and purchase money. The last of these three sections authorizes the minister having control of the lands to sign leases. The essential feature	of	the	Ordnance	and'
Admiralty Lands Act is preserved in the proposed bill. This is to the effect that all lands; required for the defence of Canada are not to be sold but may be used or occupied in such manner as the governor in council directs.
The provisions	of	the	Ordnance	andAdmiralty Lands	Act	requiring that	suchcrown lands be divided into class I and class II are dropped.	By	this	separation	into
classes, a distinction was made between public lands, the title to which could be conveyed by the crown, and those public lands in respect to which there could be no conveyance of title. The bill now before this house removes the necessity for maintaining these classes.
At the present time the only provisions relating to the correction of letters patent are in the Dominion Lands Act and these provisions apply only to the Northwest Territories and Yukon Territory. If letters patent for land in a province contain some error, it is often necessary to obtain a quit claim deed and issue another grant. The provisions relating to the correction of letters patent are therefore included in this bill in a revised form to make such provisions of general application and to prevent such delay and! expense.
A new section provides that no title in public lands shall be acquired by prescription, that is to say, by long uninterrupted usage. Title by prescription has been abolished in many provinces and the old law of prescription has no practical application today.
Upon the passing of this bill and the territorial lands bill, the Ordnance and

Public Lands Grants Act Admiralty Lands Act, the Public Lands Grants Act and the Dominion Lands Act will be repealed.

POST OFFICE-DENIAL OF THE USE OF MAILS Text of Correspondence between Mr. McTague and the Minister of Justice
WHITE, BRISTOL, GORDON, BECK & PHIPPS BARRISTERS & SOLICITORS

Hon. Charles P. McTague, K.C.,
220 Bay Street, Toronto 1, Canada, April 17th,	1950.
The Honourable Stuart Garson,
Minister of Justice,	.
Department of Justice,	*
Ottawa, Ontario.
Re: Broker Dealers Association.
As counsel for the Broker Dealers Association of Ontario and acting only in that capacity and not for any individuals concerned, I wish to put before you certain submissions with respect to the action of the Post Office Department stopping the mails to people in, or remotely associated with, the security business here in Toronto.
In the first place, my submission is that under the rule of law, to which we lawyers continually pay lip service, the procedure followed in the Post Office Department is totally without justification.
The powers of the Post Office generally in so far as they appear to be relevant to the matter alleged to be involved here are, I think, to be found in the Post Office Act, Sec. 7 (d) permitting the making of regulations, "for marking on the covering of letters, circulars or other mailable matter suspected to concern illegal lotteries, so-called gift concerts, or other illegal enterprises of like character, offering prizes,, or concerning schemes devised or intended to deceive or defraud the public, for the purpose of obtaining money under false pretences, whether such letters, circulars or other mailable matter are addressed to or received by mail from places within or without Canada, a warning that they are suspected to be of a fraudulent character and for returning such letters, circulars or other mailable matter to the senders".
The relevant regulations pursuant to Sec. 7 (d) appear to be 204 and 206, reading as follows:
204-"If it be established to the satisfaction of the Postmaster General that any person is engaged or represents himself as engaged in the business of publishing any obscene or immoral books, pamphlets, pictures, prints, engravings, lithographs, photographs or other publication, matter or thing of an indecent, immoral, seditious, disloyal, scurrilous or libellous character or in the business of an illegal lottery, so called gift concerts, or other similar enterprise offering prizes or concerning schemes devised or intended to deceive or defraud the public for the purpose of obtaining money under false pretences, or in the business of selling or in any wise disposing of counterfeit money or what is commonly called "Green Goods," or of drugs, medicines, instruments, books, papers, pamphlets, recipes, prescriptions, or other things with the object or with the pretended object of preventing conception or procuring abortion, and if such person shall, in the opinion of the Postmaster General, endeavour to use the Post Office for the promotion of such business, or if it be established to the satisfaction of the Postmaster General that any persons are using, or endeavouring to use the
Post Office for any fraudulent or illegal purpose, then, in any such case, it is hereby declared that no letters, packet, parcel, newspaper, book or other thing sent or sought to be sent through the Post Office by or on behalf of or to or on behalf of such person, shall be deemed mailable matter."
206-"The Postmaster General has power, under the statute, to mark or cause to be marked upon the covers of letters, circulars, or other mail matter suspected to concern schemes devised or intended to deceive or defraud the public for the purpose of obtaining money under false pretences, whether such letters, circulars or other mail matter are addressed to or received by mail from places within or without Canada, 'suspected to be of a fraudulent character,' and to return such letters, circulars or other mail matter to the senders."
I think you will agree that it is trite law that the regulations cannot be extended beyond the authority given in the statute to make them. For the purpose of my submission to you I am not arguing that these regulations go beyond the statutory authority for them, but I do submit as strongly as I can that the Deputy Postmaster General has gone far beyond what is provided for in the regulations or the statute in the most arbitrary way.
Without any warning whatever, and on the strength of representations made by the United States Post Office Department at the behest of the United States Securities and Exchange Commission and entirely ex parte, without the person suspected having any opportunity to be heard, the mails have not only been arbitrarily cut off, but have been required to be forwarded to Ottawa where they are held for an indefinite period without any commitment or statement of intention to prefer any charges in the courts.	Not only that, but in
separate hearings of aggrieved persons before the Deputy Postmaster General, their mail has been released upon the exaction of undertakings that they will not further deal in specified securities, or that they will agree to modify the language and terms of circulars sent in the future. The whole procedure is in substance a conviction by the Deputy Postmaster General without a hearing, punishment by cutting off the mails and the exaction of undertakings as a condition on which the penalty will be suspended.
If there is anything in the Post Office Act justifying such procedure, I am unable to locate it. In addition to that, I cannot conceive of any government putting forward legislation to justify such action by way of amendment to the Post Office Act, and I cannot conceive of any parliament enacting such legislation if it were put forward.
Mr. Turnbull seems to take undue comfort, in my opinion, in the Literary Publications Case, I think it is, in British Columbia, (58 C.C.C. 385), in giving him the right to do anything and considering that whatever he does is not reviewable by the courts. He does not seem to realize that the court in that case simply held that there was a right to exercise a discretion under the statute and the discretion having been duly and properly exercised, the courts would not review it. That case concerned an action for damages following an acquittal after a prosecution under the Criminal Code. It appears to me to be no authority for the proposition that the Post Office Department can legislate through the process of administration and in fact set up what amounts to a Star Chamber.

I recall hearing a careful speech made by yourself on the rule of law with many references to the admonitions of Coke to King James. In this affair it is McTague humbly putting forward the same type of admonition to Turnbull through your good self as an understanding intermediary, I hope.
There just cannot be two standards of fraud, one laid down by the courts and a different and private one by the Post Office Department. The Post Office Department has not, as yet, attained judicial status. It appears by its recent actions merely to assert that very untenable position.
As you know, I have had a rather wide experience in the security business. It is my opinion, and I have comparatively recently put my opinion in writing for the benefit of the United States Securities and Exchange Commission, that no provincial legislature has power to control or regulate international or interprovincial trade in securities. While I know of no case directly dealing with securities on the proposition, it has been laid down in reference to other commodities more than once that there is no such power in the province. I make brief reference to the Natural Products Marketing Board case in British Columbia.
The only jurisdiction which can validly enact legislation to control and regulate the sale of securities internationally and interprovincially is the Canadian parliament. If the policy of enacting such legislation is determined upon the government can readily put forward a statute and take its responsibility in that regard. If it does not care to accept such responsibility, surely it should not permit or even tolerate the setting up of a securities commission de facto, but certainly not de jure under the present act within the Post Office Department. Yet that is exactly what is being done at the present time.
At this time there is no law in Canada prohibiting the sale of securities in the United States by circular or otherwise. If the circular is considered to be fraudulent under the laws of Canada let prosecution be brought in the criminal courts, but let us still maintain the fundamental principle of the rule of law and once again abolish Star Chamber methods from which already too many innocent people have suffered greatly.
To stop the mails and ruin people in business on the evidence of circulars, telephone conversations and other gossip, which have taken place many months ago, seems to me a most extraordinary procedure.
I am forwarding a copy of this letter to the Right Honourable the Prime Minister and of course also to Mr. Turnbull.
Sincerely yours,
C. P. McTague.
Ottawa, Canada, May 2, 1950
The Honourable Charles P. McTague, K.C.,
220 Bay street,
Toronto 1, Ontario.
Dear Mr. McTague:
I have your letter of April 17 with reference to the action of the post office in stopping the mails of certain brokers. You are acting as counsel for the Broker Dealers Association and not on behalf of any of the persons against whom the "Stop" order was directed.
I have inquired as to what took place. The order, which was made with the approval of the Postmaster General and therefore may be regarded as made by him, was to the effect that all mails addressed to or coming from the above (persons named) are to be intercepted and sent specially by first mail to the administration branch, Ottawa. It
was stated that this action was being taken as a result of evidence received indicating that the mails were being used for the purpose of obtaining money under false pretences. I am informed that contrary to what you state in your letter the order was not made at the behest of the United States Securities and Exchange Commission.
The action was taken under the authority of paragraph (d) of section 7 of the Post Office Act which authorizes the Postmaster General to make regulations for marking on the covering of letters, circulars or other mailable matter suspected to concern . . . schemes devised or intended to deceive or defraud the public, for the purpose of obtaining money under false pretences, a warning that they are suspected to be of a fraudulent character and for returning such mailable matter to the senders. The mailable matter is marked, "Non-Transmissible" instead of with a warning that it was suspected to be of a fraudulent character. This marking was regarded as less injurious. The matter is returned to the sender.
My information is that each of the brokers named in the order was engaged in the sale of the securities of a single company. The "stop" order was made only after a careful examination was made by experienced officials of the literature which these brokers were circulating, making claims which were so extravagant and untrue as to raise a reasonable suspicion in the mind of the Postmaster General that they related to schemes intended to deceive or or defraud the public, for the purposes of obtaining money under false pretences.
I cannot discover any illegality in this procedure. The statute calls on the Postmaster General to refuse the use of the mails to persons whom he reasonably suspects of using the post office facilities to defraud the public. The only question is whether the Postmaster General had reasonable grounds for his suspicion. From the facts when they are disclosed I think you will have to agree that the Postmaster General did have good grounds for his suspicion.
Perhaps it should be remarked in this connection that none of the brokers has seen fit to take action against the Postmaster General alleging wrongful action on his part, a remedy which the court of appeal of British Columbia held, in the case of Literary Recreations Limited v. Sauve, 58 C.C.C. p. 358, to be open to a person against whom such an order has been made.
The next point made by you is that the Post Office cannot "legislate through the process of administration and in fact set up what amounts to a star chamber." I am afraid I do not follow this contention since it appears to me that the Postmaster General was doing precisely what the statute authorized and required him to do.
You point out that the province has no power to control or regulate international trade in securities. That is certainly true where the Post Office is the medium used for carrying on the international trade in securities. But I suggest that it follows from your statement that in this case the Postmaster General is the proper official and the only official who is legally qualified to exercise such control under section 7 subsection (d) of the Post Office Act.
You contend that parliament has not set up a "securities commission de facto" within the Post Office Department. I entirely agree with this contention. The Postmaster General's job is not to operate a securities commission. The Postmaster General's duty is to see that the post office facilities are not used to defraud the public. While his efforts to this end may result in protecting investors against the purchase of fraudulent securities, this result is purely consequential and is not, primarily,

his responsibility. Under the law, his statutory duty and responsibility is to maintain the efficiency and reputation of the postal services which he directs. It is for this purpose that he is empowered to stop mail which he suspects is being posted for fraudulent purposes.
As to the question whether criminal proceedings should be instituted, it is not the Postmaster General's duty to prosecute persons guilty of criminal offences. I do not need to remind you that it is the attorney general of the province who enforces the criminal law. The Postmaster General's duty is to take appropriate actions where he has reasonable grounds for suspecting that the mails are being used for fraudulent purposes.
In conclusion, I think I should say that where the state operates a public utility such as the post office, a railway or a radio station there is not thereby conferred upon each citizen an absolute right to utilize the utility, but a conditional right only, the condition being that there should be no abuse. The utility must be operated strictly for the public benefit. The government officials operating the same should have at least as wide powers to protect the public against abuse as the private owners of a public utility would have to protect their patrons. In the case of the post office, parliament has seen fit, in order to protect the service against abuse, to authorize the Postmaster General to refuse the use of mails if he has reasonable grounds for suspecting that a person is making an improper and fraudulent use of them. I am informed that this provision is one of long standing having been introduced in the act by Sir John A. Macdonald in 1889; that it has been beneficially invoked hundreds of times throughout the intervening years; and that similar provisions will be found in the post office statutes of other free countries.
Notwithstanding these facts, the government is quite open-minded with regard to this section and the powers created under it. For many months before this order was made, the government had been engaged in preparing the first general revision and consolidation of the Post Office Act since 1922. In this connection, it has been giving special attention to sections such as section 7 (d) which vest rather wide powers in the Postmaster General. We are inclined to think from the consideration which we have given this matter so far that the experience of our own post office and the post offices of other free countries over the years indicates that the power under section 7 (d) should be retained. We are also inclined to think, however, that it might perhaps be advisable that a summary appeal should be provided from the order of the Postmaster General to the courts; and that upon the hearing of this appeal the appellant should have the right to adduce any relevant evidence in addition to that upon which the Postmaster General based his order. The appellate tribunal should have power either to confirm or discharge the order of the Postmaster General. Pending the hearing and disposition of such appeal, however, the Postmaster General's order should remain in effect and should also, of course, remain in effect if confirmed by the court appealed to.
We can well understand that the organization which you represent will have well-informed views upon this subject matter and if it wishes to present a brief on any of the matters under the Post Office Act in which it has an interest, I can assure you that the government will be glad indeed to give its representations the most careful and thorough consideration.
Yours truly,
Stuart S. Garson.
Wednesday, May 10, 1950
